extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; educated lay readers interested in moral and philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or reading short, personal/philosophical essays that inspect human behavior, customs, and beliefs in a reflective, anecdotal style. Emphasis on moral observation, self-examination, and rhetorical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombastic language disconnected from substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and lofty terminology should not be used to dress up trivial matters; pompous speech that outstrips the reality of the thing is to be suspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author objects to architects and others using “bombast words” (pilasters, architraves, cornices, Corinthian and Doric orders) that summon grand images but in fact point to paltry things ("my own kitchen door"). Example quotations: “all this set out with lofty and magnificent words... the very same we make use of when we discourse of the government of an empire.” Treat talk as subordinate to real effect; beware rhetoric that substitutes appearance for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not lavish grand surnames or titles without merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Bestowment of distinguished surnames or titles should be proportional to genuine merit; indiscriminate conferral cheapens them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises the modern habit of conferring anciently-rare epithets (e.g. 'Divine' for Plato) on contemporary figures (Aretin) without comparable worth: “we make nothing of giving the surname of great to princes who have nothing more than ordinary in them.” Avoid inflated honorifics that misrepresent actual excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admire genuine frugality and modest living
rubrics_metrics.description: Parsimony and modest habits of the ancients are presented as worthy examples; simple conduct and avoidance of unnecessary expense are admirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Cato selling his warhorse to avoid shipping costs, Scipio traveling with few servants, public provision for Regulus' family. Guidance: value sober, economical behavior and the dignity of self-sufficiency as a moral good rather than ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination over outward curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: One should devote time to examining one's own abilities and defects rather than endlessly prying into others' affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne urges turning attention inward: “employ the time we spend in prying into other men’s actions... in examining our own abilities.” This is advanced as a remedy for inconstancy of desire and for attaining a clearer understanding of one's condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist inordinate appetite and aim for contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Human appetite is fickle and insatiable; one should avoid hasty grasping for novelty and practice measured enjoyment of what one has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Lucretius and Caesar, Montaigne shows that attainment does not satisfy because desire is immoderate. Guidance: curb the rush to seize; cultivate contentment and avoid always seeking the next object of desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not value rarity or difficulty over usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration for feats merely because they are rare, new, or difficult is a sign of weak judgment unless usefulness or intrinsic worth accompanies them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples (poems with every line beginning with same letter; man throwing peas through a needle's eye) and Alexander rewarding a trivial dexterity with bushels of peas. Montaigne: '’Tis a strong evidence of a weak judgment when men approve of things for their being rare and new, or for their difficulty.' Prefer usefulness and worth to mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value natural, popular poesy over middling artificiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Artless, popular poetry possesses graces comparable to perfected art; the middle, contrived sort is to be despised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises 'poesie populaire' (Gascon villanels, songs of unlettered peoples) for natural grace, while criticizing the middle sort that is neither genuinely simple nor artfully excellent. Guidance: favor sincerity and natural effect over contrived sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, natural scents; avoid masking smells with excessive perfume
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal with regard to personal scent is absence of offensive odor; excessive use of exotic perfumes may indicate a natural defect that one seeks to conceal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'their best and chiefest excellency is to be exempt from smell' and 'such as make use of fine exotic perfumes are... to be suspected of some natural imperfection.' He also values simple, natural smells and notes how odours affect spirits and health. Practical guidance: prefer cleanliness and natural scent; use incense/perfume with moderation and consider their psychological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Lord’s Prayer frequently as a fundamental devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lord's Prayer contains all necessary petitions and should be used often in private and public acts of devotion; it merits a privileged, continual place in a Christian's practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne states he would advise saying the Lord’s Prayer at sitting down and rising from table, at bed and waking, and in every action where prayer is used: 'I would that Christians always make use of the Lord’s Prayer... it is most certain that all necessary petitions are comprehended in it.' Treat it as a core, repeated devotion even if other prayers are added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayers must be accompanied by sincere purity and reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer offered while persisting in vice or without true penitence is hypocritical and may aggravate guilt; invocation of God in unjust causes is vain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'We are to have our souls pure and clean... otherwise we ourselves present Him the rods wherewith to chastise us.' He condemns those who mix devotion with execrable life and those who ask for remission without satisfaction. Guidance: ensure prayers reflect real moral change and contrition; do not use prayer as cover for vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve sacred texts and psalms for reverent, premeditated use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Psalms and sacred scripture are too holy to be turned into casual recreation or vulgar pastimes; reading scripture should be a temperate, premeditated act by select, qualified readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne objects to profaning holy texts in shops and kitchens and to indiscriminate vernacular handling: 'It is a book too serious and too venerable to be cursorily or slightly turned over.' He argues weak or ignorant readers can be harmed rather than helped. Guidance: approach scripture with preparation ('sursum corda') and restrict interpretive authority to competent persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about translating or dispersing sacred mysteries into vulgar tongues
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide dispersion of translated sacred texts may carry more danger than utility unless competent judges oversee the translation and exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne expresses worry about translating scripture into local dialects without adequate interpreters in regions (Biscay, Brittany). He notes many peoples keep their sacred language. Guidance: translations should be entrusted to capable authorities; the universal Church has solemn judgment here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputatious dialectics about core matters of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Contentious disputations can rouse heresies and are often more destructive than beneficial; acquiescence to ancient prescriptions and formulas of faith is safer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting authority and historical examples (Emperor Theodosius, Andronicus), Montaigne argues that debates and factional zeal produce schism rather than true piety. Guidance: favour prudence and moderation in theological controversy; avoid provoking public contention over sacred doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoke God with reverence and only in appropriate, just causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling on God's aid should not be habitual, careless, or used to bless unjust designs; prayer requires composed devotion and moral fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Plato and Xenophon to argue for sparing, composed invocation of the divine: 'we ought so much the more seldom to call upon God, by how much it is hard to compose our souls...'. He condemns invoking God to support vices and stresses the need for moral preparedness when praying.
